The problem with focus in general is that it behaves differently whether or not the:

- browser is actually in focus
- the actual window of the frame is in focus
- or the dev tools are open

Because of this we normalized the focus behavior (or at least attempted to) with `cy.focused()`. When you call `cy.focus()` on an element that does not receive focus due to the above listed reasons - we not only normalize the event and fire all of the appropriate events but we keep track of the state of the 'focused' element internally. That enables us to then fire the proper 'blur' events when the element should have lost focus.

What we do is basically a polyfill for when the browser doesn't do the "right thing" just because its out of focus. 

I believe there was a specific technical reason we chose not to implement `have.focus` in the chai-jquery rewrite, but I can't remember what it was. 

The problem is that because we are normalizing focus it means Cypress is the only source of truth to understand what *should* be in focus even when its not. Because of that - the `have.focus` assertion would have to call into the Cypress machinery and could not use anything else. It would basically just be the same thing as the yielded result from `cy.focused()`.

We have some internal notes in the driver about exposing a new  configuration like: 
```
{ wrapDomElementsWithJQuery: false }
```

This would then prevent Cypress from *ever* wrapping any DOM elements it encounters in jquery - and instead pass everything along. Our internal command signatures would not change (they'd have to accommodate both object types) but when yielding the elements you'd need to update your code.

However I think this doesn't really solve your problem - it seems you probably want to *keep* the wrapping of jquery, but be able to lean into the native elements when you want to.

The problem is that Cypress will continually re-wrap DOM elements whenever they are returned as the subject of a command.  This is to ensure that internally Cypress always understands the type. It even converts jquery objects *from your application* back into our own. That's the only way we can control them deterministically.

If we didn't do that you could write this code:

```js
cy.get('element').invoke('get', 0).invoke('checkValidity')
```

The problem is that `invoke('get', 0)` will unroll the native DOM element but then it'll be wrapped back up when the next `invoke` runs.

I think currently it's not really that big of a deal to utilize a `then` or `should` to explicitly call what you're trying to do.

You cite that the command log is the problem here - that you cannot easily tell because its comparing booleans instead of objects. That would still be the case here with my example above. Chaining the `should` to the `invoke('checkValidity')` would still change the subject to be boolean and not DOM. So that wouldn't really help you.

Even in its current state the Command Log does in fact help provide visual reference for the assertion. Notice how the assertion is indented? It knows that the assertion is about the current subject: the `<input>`.

My final thought is that if you *did* want to assert in regards to something about the element then you'd need to add a chai assertion plugin. Something like `cy.get('input').should('be.valid'). You would then make that assertion do the right thing and could call whatever methods you like but keep the subject as the element reference.

That's exactly what we've done for all DOM based assertions here:

This is a pretty good start.

Couple things...

There are a bunch of built in stringifier functions in Cypress.

They do slightly different things and are used in a bunch of places in the driver...

```js
Cypress.utils.stringify(...)
Cypress.utils.stringifyArg(...)
Cypress.utils.stringifyActual(...)
```

The bigger problem with your custom command is that based on the way you've written this you've made it mostly impossible to retry assertions until they pass.

Why?

Well in the built in Cypress commands - each command has to decide **how** and if it should retry, and of course whether it has any built in default assertions.

There is an API for this but it has not been documented nor 100% formalized.

By returning the `cy.wrap` command at the very end - you're then passing off the `result` value to `cy.wrap` which then ends up utilizing the retry code built into that command.

That means that your assertions are actually chained to the `cy.wrap` and it will retry them until the pass.

The problem is that once you pass off an immutable value like a `Boolean` then retrying becomes worthless.

`cy.wrap` could not possibly do anything because its just been handed a value - it has no idea where it came from or anything.

I actually cannot think of a way to make this work using what you have available at the moment. We likely need to bite the bullet and document the retry API's.

Today I would just recommend looking at the driver code to see how `invoke` or `wrap` is created and then using those API's. We wrote them to be publicly available. You'll then have to implement your own retry logic. It's not that hard but you'll have to do some legwork.

However, this is not necessarily indicative of any kind of memory leak. The system task manager will not provide you a reliable means of calculating memory because of the way garbage collection works in the browser. Browsers will prime and hold onto object references way beyond whether or not they should be garbage collected. There is **no** way to force GC (without running Chrome in a specific mode). It's up to the browser to choose when and how it runs GC. 

To figure out a real memory usage you either need to use the Timeline Profiler which forces GC every 100ms or so. This mode will make Cypress tests run unimaginably slow which makes it somewhat difficult to use. The other option is to monitor the Chrome Task Manager.

You have to look at Javascript Memory - and more specifically the numbers in parenthesis. What this is distinguishing is **primed** memory as well as memory that's scheduled to be GC. You will see growth for each test that runs but then when you "rerun" the entire suite, it will drop back down temporarily before going back up again.

The real issue here is what I've described many times before. There is an entire proposal that goes into a lot of detail:  https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/681#issue-259623204

It is simply this...

### You cannot use the GUI to run all of your tests.

That's the problem and the solution. You cannot run all of your tests. The GUI is a mode built specifically to run one or a small number of tests at a time.

Cypress is capturing snapshots of the DOM for every single command which uses up a massive amount of memory. Why does it do this? So you can debug your tests and application as you iterate on a single or small number of tests at a time. The GUI is not built to handle entire runs.

Currently you can tell Cypress to cleanup snapshots by setting the `{ numTestsKeptInMemory: 0 }` in `cypress.json`. This will purge snapshots aggressively but then you will lose the ability to debug any of your tests. 

If you want to run all your tests you need to do it from the command line using `cypress run`. In that mode it makes specific performance optimizations (like not taking snapshots) because it knows you're not iterating on a test or working with the results.

The problem is most definitely that the Windows site is not under your control and has employed security restrictions that prevent Cypress from working.

Visiting or interacting with 3rd party content is a common anti-pattern and the workaround is to always use `cy.request` for interacting with the party in order to isolate getting just the token part.

I think you are on the right track that you should just set the cookie / session stuff directly (and that will work). If you're being redirected by the client or server it's likely due to it **not** having the right session information to work. Perhaps the cookies are domain based cookies instead of host-only.

Check to see if Windows has a published SSO API that you can use directly with `cy.request`. I am sure they do. Use those API's and you'll avoid ever needing your UI to utilize their services - which insulates you from changes on their end. It'll also make testing much much faster.

Here's the anti pattern for reference.

https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/best-practices.html#Visiting-External-Sites

Also please check out our SSO recipes that show this in action.

https://docs.cypress.io/examples/recipes/logging-in-recipe.html#Single-Sign-On

I'm going to close this issue as there is nothing that can be done on our part. We could deploy strategies to remove the javascript code causing Cypress to be redirected but even if we did there is a better approach and you shouldn't ever use the UI to accomplish this.

P.S. `chromeWebSecurity` is detailed in the following guide.

https://docs.cypress.io/guides/guides/web-security.html

All it does is remove cross origin restrictions. That's all it does. The host site can still deploy certain restrictions that prevent Cypress from working. These are all in `javascript` and it goes against our testing philosophy to try to bypass these. Whenever users come across these problems it is *always* indicative of a testing anti-pattern. Think of it as "good barriers".
